summary: Dominica is a volcanic island nation in the Caribbean, known for its pristine rainforest, hot springs and the “Boiling Lake,” and is one of the few Caribbean countries that still has a Kalinago indigenous territory.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In the 18th century French settlers moved to Dominica from Martinique and Guadeloupe to clear land and brought Catholic missionaries, and some of the indigenous Kalinago also converted. Although the island passed to Britain after the Treaty of Paris in 1763, the French-descended residents and their African slave communities had already formed a firm Catholic tradition, which Britain did not suppress, so Catholicism remains the largest religion to this day.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: After British rule was established, the Anglican Church became the official colonial church, and in the 1780s Methodist missionaries also came to the island and grew among slaves and freed people of African descent. From the 20th century, Seventh-day Adventist and American-origin Pentecostal churches grew rapidly, bringing the Protestant share close to three-tenths.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Dominican society is strongly religious, and churches play an important role in education and community life, so the proportion of the non-religious is not high, mainly young people influenced by urbanization and life overseas.

ranking.name: Rastafari
ranking.description: Rastafari originated in Jamaica in the 1930s, reached Dominica in the 1970s and attracted many young people. At the time the government regarded it as a social threat, and in 1974 it passed a law popularly known as the “Dread Act” that harshly suppressed it, provoking long-running controversy; believers remain a minority to this day.

religion.background: In the 17th–18th centuries Dominica was an island repeatedly contested by Britain and France; French settlers brought Catholicism, and after the island passed to British rule in 1763 Anglicanism and Methodism were introduced. Africans trafficked under slavery received Christianity within two colonial cultures, and the indigenous Kalinago were gradually influenced as well. After independence in 1978, Catholicism remained in the majority with the Protestant denominations coexisting, and Rastafari, introduced in the late 20th century, was for a time suppressed by the government.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: Dominica came under British rule from 1763, British control was secure after 1805, and English became the language of administration, law and schooling. At independence in 1978 English was made the official language, government, media and formal settings operate in English, and the younger generation and urban residents use English as their main language.

ranking.name: Dominican Creole French (Kwéyòl)
ranking.description: In the 18th century French planters and their West African slaves formed a French-based Creole on the island. Although English was promoted after the British took over, rural residents continued to use Creole as their everyday language, which has lasted more than two hundred years. From the 1980s a grassroots preservation movement arose, and every October “Creole Day” (Jounen Kwéyòl) is marked with broadcasts, music and food, but the proportion of young people who use it is gradually declining.

language.history: The indigenous Kalinago originally spoke an Arawakan language of the Caribbean islands, which gradually died out after colonization. In the 18th century French settlers and African slaves formed a French Creole here, mutually intelligible with the Creoles of Martinique, Guadeloupe and Saint Lucia. British rule after 1763 made English the official and educational language, creating a bilingual society with English above and Creole below. After independence the government gradually recognized the cultural value of Creole, but English remains the main language for education and employment.

ranking.name: Callaloo soup
ranking.description: Dasheen (taro) leaves or amaranth leaves are stewed with okra, coconut milk, onion and spices into a thick green soup, sometimes with crab or salted meat added.
ranking.history: This kind of thick leafy-green soup originated in West Africa; slaves trafficked to the Caribbean recreated the stewed greens of their homeland with local taro leaves and okra, with a different version on each island. Dominica’s original national dish was a “mountain chicken” dish made from the giant frog, but from 2002 chytridiomycosis brought this frog close to extinction, so callaloo soup has come to be regarded more often as the representative national dish. It is a signature dish of Sunday family lunches and festivals.

ranking.name: Bakes (fried dough)
ranking.description: Flour, baking powder, salt and water are kneaded into a dough, pressed into small rounds and fried or baked, crisp outside and soft inside, often filled with saltfish or cheese for breakfast.
ranking.history: The appearance of fried bakes is linked to the flour imported during the British colonial period, when colonial residents used cheap imported flour to make a bread that could quickly fill the stomach; it is also called “johnny cake,” one account holding that it derives from the “journey cake” carried on trips. Its most classic way of eating is with saltfish for breakfast, and it remains the most common breakfast and school snack among Dominicans.

ranking.name: Saltfish
ranking.description: Salt-cured dried cod is soaked in water to remove the salt and then stir-fried with onion, tomato and chili, and is often eaten with fried bakes or boiled breadfruit.
ranking.history: Salted cod came from Newfoundland and other places in the North Atlantic, and in the 18th century was shipped to the Caribbean in large quantities in the British-led triangular trade; because it was cheap and kept well, planters used it as the protein ration for slaves. Although the Caribbean is rich in fresh fish, this colonial-era import became deeply integrated into the local diet. Today “saltfish with bakes” is Dominica’s most representative breakfast.

ranking.name: Breadfruit
ranking.description: Breadfruit is a large, starchy fruit that can be boiled, roasted, fried or made into a salad, with a texture like potato or bread.
ranking.history: Breadfruit is native to the Pacific islands. In 1789 the British captain Bligh, in order to carry it to the Caribbean as cheap food for slaves, met a mutiny of his crew aboard the Bounty; he sailed again later and in 1793 successfully delivered saplings to Saint Vincent and Jamaica, and from there it spread to Dominica and other islands. This crop, introduced for the colonial economy, later became an important staple for islanders in times of food shortage such as after hurricanes.

ranking.name: Cassava bread (Kasavé)
ranking.description: Cassava is grated and its toxic juice pressed out, then the cassava flour is spread on an iron griddle and baked into a large thin flatbread, crisp or slightly chewy, plain or with coconut.
ranking.history: Cassava bread is a traditional food of the indigenous Kalinago; long before Europeans arrived, the indigenous people of the Caribbean knew how to remove the cyanide from bitter cassava and bake it into bread. In 1903 Britain designated a Kalinago Territory on the east coast of the island, where residents still make cassava bread in the traditional way and sell it to tourists. It represents the cultural tradition preserved by Dominica as one of the few Caribbean islands that still has an indigenous community.
